title: Valid consent and refusal
blurb: Check that consent is voluntary, informed and given with capacity, and respond correctly when someone refuses or withdraws.
question: Mr Bello, 30, agreed to a urinary catheter. Partway through insertion he becomes distressed and says, "Stop, I don't want this." He has capacity. What should the nurse do?

teach.body: For consent to be valid it must be given voluntarily, by an appropriately informed person, who has the capacity to consent to the intervention in question. Acquiescence when the person does not know what the intervention involves is not consent. In plain English: they chose freely, they knew what they were agreeing to, and they were able to decide. The Code adds: get properly informed consent and document it before carrying out any action (4.2).
teach.cite: DH Reference guide to consent (2nd ed, 2009) ch 1 para 1; Code 4.2

teach.h: Valid consent sits where all three overlap
teach.caption: A signature on a form cannot rescue consent that fails any of the three.

teach.body: Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board (2015) requires reasonable care to make sure the person knows about any material risks and reasonable alternatives. A risk is material if a reasonable person in their position would attach significance to it, or the clinician knows, or should know, that this particular person would. So a small risk to finger sensation matters to a professional violinist even if most people would shrug it off.
teach.cite: Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board [2015] UKSC 11

teach.caption: The validity of consent does not depend on its form; written consent is evidence, and good practice for significant procedures.

teach.h: When a person withdraws consent during a procedure
teach.caption: A person with capacity may withdraw consent at any time, including during a procedure (DH guide ch 1 para 45).

teach.h: Scenario: Mrs Adeyemi refuses her dressing
teach.body: Mrs Adeyemi, 72, has capacity and a leg ulcer. When Nurse Joy arrives to change the dressing she says firmly she does not want it done today. Joy respects the refusal, asks why (it hurt last time), explains the risks of leaving it, offers pain relief and another time, and records the conversation. Code 2.5: respect, support and document a person's right to accept or refuse care.

head: Age
Position
rows: Adult; presumed to have capacity (MCA s1(2))
Presumed capable of consenting to own treatment (FLRA 1969 s8)
teach.caption: A competent 16 or 17-year-old's refusal may in certain circumstances be overridden by a person with parental responsibility or a court.

items: Watch for pressure from partners, family or staff to accept or refuse.
Where appropriate, see the person on their own to check the decision is truly theirs.
Pressure to agree is not a reason to doubt capacity: capacity is still presumed.
Use a professional interpreter, not family, so information and choice are genuine (Code 7.2).

teach.text: Don't confuse 'unwise' with 'invalid'. A person with capacity who makes a voluntary, informed refusal must be respected, even if the outcome may be serious. And don't sign up someone else's patient: the clinician providing the treatment is responsible for ensuring valid consent, so a nurse should not take consent for a procedure she cannot explain.

items: Valid consent: voluntary, informed, with capacity; acquiescence is not consent.
Montgomery: material risks and reasonable alternatives, judged from the person's point of view.
Implied, verbal and written consent can all be valid; document it (Code 4.2).
Consent can be withdrawn at any time: stop, explore, explain, respect, record (Code 2.5).
16-17s are presumed capable; under-16s can consent if Gillick competent.

summary: You can now test any consent against the three requirements, explain Montgomery's standard of information, recognise implied, verbal and written consent, and handle a refusal or withdrawal of consent in line with Code 2.5 and 4.2.

A.q: The nurse explains to Mr Lewis, 64, that she needs a blood sample to check his kidney function. He nods, rolls up his sleeve and holds out his arm. What type of consent is this?
options: Written consent
Presumed consent
Implied consent
Proxy consent
A.why: After an explanation, holding out an arm shows agreement by conduct: implied (non-verbal) consent. It is valid because it is voluntary, informed and given with capacity (DH guide ch 1 para 35).

whyNot.1: Presumed consent assumes agreement without any indication; here he has shown it.
whyNot.3: Proxy consent is given by someone else on a person's behalf.

A.q: Ms Novak, 45, is a professional violinist due to have a hand operation. Under Montgomery (2015), which risks must she be told about?
options: Those a responsible body of surgeons would usually mention to patients
Those she, or a reasonable person in her position, would think significant
Those occurring in more than 1 in 100 operations of this particular type
Those that are recorded on the trust's standard consent form for this operation
A.why: Montgomery: a risk is material if a reasonable person in the patient's position would attach significance to it, or the clinician knows or should know this patient would. A small risk to finger sensation is material to a violinist.

whyNot.0: This is the older professional-practice standard that Montgomery replaced for information-giving.
whyNot.2: Montgomery sets no percentage threshold; materiality depends on the person.
whyNot.3: A standard form may omit risks that are material to this particular person.

A.q: Ms Clarke, 38, agrees verbally to a wound swab after the nurse explains why it is needed. Which action completes the nurse's duty under Code 4.2?
options: Asking Ms Clarke to sign a consent form before the swab
Asking a colleague to witness the verbal consent
Repeating the explanation after the swab is taken
Documenting the consent in Ms Clarke's records
A.why: Code 4.2: get properly informed consent and document it before carrying out any action. Verbal consent is valid for a wound swab; the record shows it was obtained.

whyNot.0: A form is not needed for a simple swab; verbal consent is valid.
whyNot.1: A witness is not required for verbal consent to a routine procedure.
whyNot.2: Consent must be informed before the procedure, not explained afterwards.

B.q: Partway through catheter insertion, Mr Bello, 30, who has capacity, becomes distressed and says, "Stop, I don't want this." What should the nurse do?
options: Finish quickly, as stopping halfway is more uncomfortable
Stop, then explore his concerns and explain the options
Pause, offer reassurance and then carry on with the procedure
Ask a colleague to hold his hand while she completes it
B.why: A person with capacity can withdraw consent at any time, including during a procedure. Good practice is to stop if possible, establish the concerns and explain the consequences (DH guide ch 1 para 45; Code 2.5).

whyNot.0: Continuing after clear withdrawal of consent by a person with capacity is unlawful touching.
whyNot.2: Carrying on after a pause without fresh consent ignores his withdrawal.
whyNot.3: Comfort does not replace consent; he has said stop.

B.q: A surgical registrar asks Nurse Priya to get Mrs Kaur's signature on a consent form for a laparoscopic procedure tomorrow. Priya has not been trained in the procedure. What should she do?
options: Get the signature, as the registrar has explained it already
Ask Mrs Kaur to sign and pass any questions to the registrar
Decline and ask the registrar to seek consent from Mrs Kaur
Witness the form once Mrs Kaur says she understands it
B.why: The clinician providing the treatment is responsible for valid consent; the task may be delegated only to someone with sufficient knowledge of the procedure and its risks (DH guide para 30). Code 13.3: ask for help with anything beyond your competence.

whyNot.0: Priya cannot confirm Mrs Kaur is informed about risks she cannot explain herself.
whyNot.1: Collecting a signature without being able to answer questions does not make consent informed.
whyNot.3: Witnessing a form does not make consent valid if the information was not given properly.

B.q: Mrs Oyelaran, 79, is being discharged to a care home. Her son repeatedly says in front of her that she 'has to go' and answers questions for her. What should the nurse do first?
options: Arrange a formal capacity assessment for the decision
Proceed, as her son holds the closest relationship
Ask the social worker to make the decision instead
Speak with Mrs Oyelaran alone to explore her wishes
B.why: Consent must be voluntary, without undue influence; where appropriate see the person alone to establish that the decision is truly theirs (DH guide ch 1 para 10). Capacity is still presumed (MCA s1(2)).

whyNot.0: Pressure from a relative is not a reason to doubt capacity.
whyNot.1: A relative's view does not replace the decision of a person presumed to have capacity.
whyNot.2: The decision belongs to Mrs Oyelaran unless she is shown to lack capacity.

C.q: Mr Tran, 52, speaks little English and is due to have a chest drain inserted today. His 14-year-old son offers to translate the consent discussion. What should the nurse arrange?
options: A professional interpreter for the consent discussion
His son, with the doctor checking key words are understood
A translated leaflet, with his son to answer questions
A bilingual porter who has offered to help translate
C.why: Consent must be informed (Montgomery 2015), so Mr Tran needs to understand risks and alternatives. Code 7.2 and NHS England interpreting guidance (2018): use a professional interpreter; children should not interpret except for immediate necessary treatment.

whyNot.1: A child should not interpret a consent discussion for a planned procedure.
whyNot.2: A leaflet plus a child interpreter does not ensure informed consent.
whyNot.3: A porter is not a trained interpreter and may translate inaccurately; a professional interpreter should be used.

C.q: Josh, 16, has capacity and agrees to have a wound sutured in the emergency department. His mother is not present. Which statement is correct in England?
options: He can consent, as 16 and 17-year-olds are presumed capable
He can consent, but his mother must countersign the record
He cannot consent until a parent has been contacted by phone
He can consent if a doctor first confirms Gillick competence
C.why: Family Law Reform Act 1969 s8: people aged 16 or 17 are presumed capable of consenting to their own medical treatment (DH guide ch 3).

whyNot.1: No parental countersignature is required for a 16-year-old's valid consent.
whyNot.2: Parental contact is not a precondition for a capable 16-year-old to consent.
whyNot.3: Gillick competence is the test for under-16s; at 16 he is presumed capable.

C.q: Mr Okafor, 67, has capacity. After a clear explanation of the risks, he refuses a blood transfusion for religious reasons, although he may die without it. What is the correct response?
options: Treat him in his best interests, as the refusal is life-threatening
Ask his family to persuade him, then reassess his capacity
Respect the refusal, document it and continue other care
Give the transfusion if he loses consciousness later on
C.why: A voluntary, informed refusal by an adult with capacity must be respected even where it may result in death (DH guide ch 1 para 44; Code 2.5). An unwise decision does not mean incapacity (MCA s1(4)).

whyNot.0: Best interests decisions apply to people who lack capacity; he has capacity.
whyNot.1: Arranging persuasion undermines voluntariness, and the refusal is not grounds to question capacity.
whyNot.3: His capacitous refusal still stands; losing consciousness does not cancel it.

reteach.title: Consent is a conversation, not a signature
reteach.question: If a signature on a form isn't consent, what is?

blocks.body: Did they choose freely? (no pressure from family or staff). Do they know what they're agreeing to, including risks that matter to them and the alternatives? Can they make this decision? If all three are yes, consent is valid whether it is a nod, a 'yes' or a signature. If any is no, no form can fix it. And consent can be taken back at any time.

blocks.text: A refusal by an adult with capacity stands even if it is unwise and life-threatening.

explain.body: Consent must be given freely, without pressure or undue influence to accept or refuse, whether from family or staff. Where appropriate, see the person alone (DH guide ch 1 para 10).

test.q: A husband insists his wife will have the operation and speaks over her. What does this most threaten?
options: The voluntariness of her consent
Her capacity to make the decision
The written form of her consent
The materiality of the risks
test.why: Pressure from a partner threatens voluntariness; she should be seen alone.

whyNot.1: Pressure from others does not mean she lacks capacity.
whyNot.2: The form of consent is not the issue.
whyNot.3: Materiality concerns information about risks, not pressure.

explain.body: Montgomery (2015): tell the person about material risks and reasonable alternatives. Materiality is judged by a reasonable person in their position, or what you know matters to them.

test.q: Under Montgomery, materiality of a risk is judged from whose perspective?
options: A responsible body of clinicians in that specialty
The trust's consent policy
A reasonable person in the patient's position
The clinician who will do the procedure
test.why: Materiality is judged by what a reasonable person in the patient's position, or this particular patient, would consider significant.

whyNot.0: That is the professional standard Montgomery replaced for information.
whyNot.3: The clinician's own view is not the test.

explain.body: Consent may be implied, verbal or written. The form does not make consent valid; it is evidence. Written consent is good practice for significant procedures. Always document (Code 4.2).

test.q: A patient signs a consent form but was not told of a material risk. Is the consent valid?
options: Yes, because the form has been signed
Yes, if a witness also signed the form
No, because it was not properly informed
No, because verbal consent was also needed
test.why: A signature does not make consent valid if the person was not appropriately informed (DH guide ch 1 para 32).

whyNot.0: A signature is evidence only, not validity.
whyNot.1: A witness does not cure missing information.
whyNot.3: Written consent does not also require verbal consent.

explain.body: An adult with capacity may refuse or withdraw consent at any time, even during a procedure and even if the outcome may be serious. Stop, explore, explain consequences, respect and record (Code 2.5).

test.q: A patient with capacity refuses physiotherapy after hip surgery. What should the nurse do?
options: Arrange a formal capacity assessment because the refusal is unwise
Explore the reasons, explain the risks and record the refusal
Ask the physiotherapist to return in an hour and try again
Inform the family so they can encourage the patient
test.why: Code 2.5: respect, support and document the right to refuse; exploring reasons may reveal a fixable problem such as pain.

whyNot.0: An unwise decision is not grounds to assume incapacity (MCA s1(4)).
whyNot.2: Planning a repeat attempt without exploring the reasons does not respect or address the refusal.
whyNot.3: Involving family without consent breaches confidentiality and adds pressure.
